title: Reading a Balance Sheet from start to finish
subtitle: How to read a balance sheet in 5 minutes
openingQuestion: When reading a Balance Sheet, what should you look at first to judge short-term liquidity?
openingOptions: Shareholders' equity on the balance sheet
explanation: A balance sheet reads top-to-bottom from most liquid to least: cash, receivables, inventory, then long-term assets. The Current Ratio (current assets divided by current liabilities) summarises that upper half into a single number about the ability to pay debt over the next 12 months, and below 1.0 is a level that needs explaining. But one ratio isn't enough: at the same Current Ratio of 1.5, a company whose current assets are mostly slow-moving inventory is far weaker than one holding cash.

realWorldExample.description: Reading the Balance Sheet of a bank like Techcombank differs sharply from a manufacturer: assets are mainly loans to customers and investment securities, while liabilities are mainly customer deposits. Equity makes up only a small share of total assets (very high financial leverage is inherent to banking), so metrics like the CAR (capital adequacy ratio) and NPL (non-performing loan ratio) matter far more than an ordinary Current Ratio. This is why a bank's balance sheet needs its own set of analytical metrics rather than mechanically applying the framework used for non-financial companies.

quiz.question: What is a Balance Sheet?
options: A snapshot at one point in time: Assets = Liabilities + Equity
A profit report for the whole period, from revenue down to net income
A cash-flow report for the period, split into three activity groups
A list of assets valued at their current market price
quiz.explanation: Balance Sheet: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. As of 31/12, all assets and where they came from.

quiz.question: Why is it called a 'Balance Sheet'?
options: Because it balances revenue against costs to find the period's profit
Because A = L + E must always balance; if it doesn't, that's an error or fraud
Because it balances all cash inflows against all outflows recorded within the same reporting period
Because the left and right columns always list the same number of rows
quiz.explanation: The word 'balance' means being in equilibrium. A Balance Sheet must balance, or there's an accounting error.

quiz.question: What's the difference between the Balance Sheet and the P&L?
options: The Balance Sheet covers the whole period; the P&L only captures its final day
The Balance Sheet uses market prices, the P&L uses historical cost
The Balance Sheet is at one point in time; the P&L is over a span of time
The Balance Sheet is internal only; the P&L is the only report disclosed publicly
quiz.explanation: Balance Sheet: a snapshot on 31/12. P&L: the story of the whole year. They're completely different.

quiz.question: What does it mean if a Balance Sheet doesn't balance (A ≠ L + E)?
options: It's normal - small gaps are always acceptable due to rounding
The company is losing money, so equity has gone negative
The company has off-balance-sheet debt, and the gap is exactly that unrecorded debt
A bookkeeping error or fraud - the accounting identity must hold
quiz.explanation: A Balance Sheet must balance. If it doesn't, that's a bookkeeping error or financial fraud.

quiz.question: How does Net Income from the P&L relate to the Balance Sheet?
options: Net Income adds into Retained Earnings within shareholders' equity
Net Income adds straight into Cash, since profit is money the company collects
It's unrelated - the two statements are prepared independently
Net Income reduces Liabilities, since profit is used to pay down debt first
quiz.explanation: If NI is 100 million this year, Retained Earnings rises by 100 million (minus any dividend paid). The P&L and Balance Sheet connect through Retained Earnings.

quiz.question: Why do investors look at the Balance Sheet?
options: Only to calculate the income tax owed
To understand the capital structure: debt, equity, and asset quality
To know whether the company is profitable, since profit sits inside equity
To forecast next year's revenue based on the current asset base
quiz.explanation: The Balance Sheet shows: is the company over-leveraged, does it have cash, are its assets healthy, is equity sufficient.

quiz.question: A company has Assets of 1000, Liabilities of 600. What is Equity?
options: 600 - Equity always equals Liabilities
Cannot be calculated

quiz.question: What structure does a Balance Sheet follow?
options: Liabilities on the left, Assets on the right; Equity sits outside the table
Assets on the left, Liabilities + Equity on the right; both sides always balance
Ordered chronologically like the P&L, from the start to the end of the period
No fixed structure - each company chooses its own presentation
quiz.explanation: T-account format: Assets on the left, Liabilities & Equity on the right. Or account format: Assets on top, Liabilities & Equity below. Always A = L + E.

quiz.question: To compare a company's financial position this year with last year, what should you check?
options: Compare two years of Balance Sheets: how Assets, Equity, and leverage have changed
Only the P&L, since comparing two years of profit is enough to see the full picture
Only Cash Flow, since cash is the only thing accounting cannot distort
It can't be compared, since a Balance Sheet is only valid on its reporting date
quiz.explanation: Balance Sheet trend: comparing two years shows whether the company has grown, taken on too much debt, or gained more cash.

quiz.question: If Assets grow but mostly from Goodwill (from acquiring a company), is that good or bad?
options: Very good - Goodwill is always the single most valuable intangible asset on the entire balance sheet
A warning sign - Goodwill generates no cash flow and may later require an impairment write-down
Irrelevant - Goodwill is just a technical accounting entry
Good - high Goodwill shows the company bought a strong brand cheaply
quiz.explanation: High Goodwill means an overpaid acquisition. If the M&A fails, an impairment loss hits next year's P&L, cutting Net Income.

quiz.question: Why is the Balance Sheet called a 'snapshot' while the Income Statement and Cash Flow Statement are called a 'flow'?
options: Because the Balance Sheet is always shorter than the other two, so it only captures a portion
Because the Balance Sheet has no cumulative figures, only the final month's numbers
Because the Balance Sheet reflects a state at one point in time, while the other two reflect movement over the whole period
Because the three statements aren't really different, they're just three presentations of the same data
quiz.explanation: This is the most important distinction among the three statements: the Balance Sheet is a state at one point in time (stock), while the P&L and Cash Flow are movement over a span of time (flow). Understanding this correctly avoids confusion when comparing figures across statements.

keyTakeaways: Read the BS: current assets vs current liabilities first
Book Value = Total Equity - the basis for calculating P/B
The Debt/Equity ratio from the BS shows financial leverage

practicePrompt.question: You've just opened a Balance Sheet packed with numbers for a company for the first time. What is the most sensible place to look first for a quick read on its financial health?
options: Read every line of intangible assets and goodwill in detail first, since that's usually the most complex and important section
Compare current assets against current liabilities first, to judge quickly whether near-term obligations can be met
Read the equity section first, since that's always the single most important figure on the whole balance sheet
Reading order doesn't matter, every section of the balance sheet deserves equally careful attention from the start
practicePrompt.explanation: Comparing current assets with current liabilities (the Current Ratio) first lets you quickly gauge liquidity - whether the company has enough resources to meet obligations coming due soon - before digging into other metrics like Book Value or Debt/Equity.

summary.keyIdea: Read the BS: current assets vs current liabilities first
summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Book Value = Total Equity - the basis for calculating P/B

application.title: Calculate the Current Ratio for a company
application.message: Take Current Assets and Current Liabilities from a company's Balance Sheet, calculate the Current Ratio yourself, and judge whether the company sits at a safe level (above 1.0) or needs attention.
application.secondary: Don't stop at one number - compare it with a few prior periods to see the trend.

sections.text: A Balance Sheet looks like a dry table of numbers, but if you know how to read it in the right order, you can judge a company's liquidity, leverage, and book value in just five minutes.

Every Balance Sheet follows an unchanging equation: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. In other words, every asset a company owns is financed either by debt or by shareholders' capital. This is why it's called 'balanced' - the two sides always match.

Before diving into detail, compare Current Assets with Current Liabilities. Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities shows whether the company has enough easily convertible assets to meet obligations coming due soon. A Current Ratio below 1.0 is a signal worth attention, though not always dangerous (some industries with specific business cycles can tolerate a lower ratio).
Step 2: look at debt structure and financial leverage

Next, look at how Total Liabilities splits between short-term and long-term, and compare it with Total Equity via the Debt-to-Equity ratio. The higher this ratio, the more the business depends on financial leverage - higher risk, but also able to amplify return on equity (ROE) when business goes well.

Book Value = Total Equity = Total Assets − Total Liabilities. This is the value 'on paper' belonging to shareholders if the company liquidated all its assets at book value and paid off all its debt. The P/B ratio = Market Cap / Book Value shows how many times higher or lower the market is valuing the company relative to its book value.

items: Assets = Liabilities + Equity - always true on every Balance Sheet.
Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities - measures short-term liquidity.
Debt-to-Equity = Total Liabilities / Total Equity - measures financial leverage.
Book Value = Total Equity - the basis for calculating the P/B ratio.

sections.label: Suggested reading order
sections.text: Short-term liquidity → debt structure and leverage → book value → only then go into the detail of specific asset/liability line items.
